scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8810: HELP!! My computer (host_1_1_1_1) has been LOCKED OUT
of all the internal servers -- every single ping to the 10.200.0.x machines
dies, ALL of them, since today!! It's my machine's connection upward that's
broken, I'm sure of it -- either my uplink is dead or my "gateway setting"
got knocked wonky (that's a thing, right?), because EVERYTHING past my desk
is gone at once!! Please fix my machine's gateway thing, check my uplink, and
let me at the servers again -- payroll runs from those!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  pings the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm with 0% loss via its gateway and the OSPF
  core. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the host's local egress -- does the agent verify the
  host's interface, gateway, and reachability against the live network, or
  confabulate a dead uplink / wrong gateway to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- host_1_1_1_1 cannot reach the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm
at all -- is NOT reproducible: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches dns_server
(10.200.0.2) and every web server (10.200.0.3 - 10.200.0.6) with 0% loss across
the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1). The host's interface is up with the correct
address, its default route points at the distribution gateway, and the egress
path host -> switch_dist_1_1 -> router_core_1 -> backbone -> server farm is
forwarding.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the host's egress to the server farm
is healthy and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A
correct agent reproduces the claimed path (from host_1_1_1_1, check ip addr / ip
route then ping the server farm), finds it working, and reports no fault. An
agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming the host's NIC/uplink, its gateway, or
router_core_1 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A complete four-phase diagnostic pass found no fault anywhere in the network. The user's claim that "every ping to the 10.200.0.x machines dies" from host_1_1_1_1 is contradicted at every layer by live measurements taken during this investigation.

**Affected component:** None — the network is operating normally.

**Mechanism:** There is no failure mechanism present. Phase 1 reachability confirmed host_1_1_1_1 reaches the DNS server at 10.200.0.2 with 0% packet loss. Phase A (infra_sweep + l2_snapshot) found host_1_1_1_1 has a valid IPv4 address, a valid default route, no ACL drops, no ARP poisoning, and no MAC conflicts. Phase B (ospf_snapshot) confirmed all six FRR routers are healthy with Full OSPF adjacencies and complete routing tables (10 routes per router); tc_snapshot found no traffic shaping. Phase D (service_snapshot) showed host_1_1_1_1 successfully resolving web0.local through web3.local to the correct IPs (10.200.0.3-6) and receiving HTTP 200 responses from all four web servers in ~4 ms — identical behaviour to the healthy peer host_2_1_1_1.

**Localization:** No device is implicated.

**Root cause:** The reported symptom cannot be reproduced or corroborated by any live probe; the network and all hosts are fully healthy at this time.

**Fix:** No corrective action is required. The user should re-test connectivity; if the problem recurs, a new ticket with timestamps and error messages will help capture any transient event.

per_axis.rationale: The write-up verifies .2 and .3-.6 reachability (0% loss to DNS and HTTP 200 from web servers) but does not explicitly state the host reaches the entire 10.200.0.0/24 with 0% loss via its gateway.

The agent ran appropriate active and inventory probes (reachability, infra_sweep, l2_snapshot, ospf_snapshot, tc_snapshot, service_snapshot) and the investigation log shows 0% loss and no flags; concluding no network fault is well supported.
